## Motivation

11/17/20 Los Alamos National Laboratory

## • BaF2 is one of the fastest known

## scintillators, emitting at 220 nm with sub-nanosecond decay constant [1]

## – Excellent for timing applications • 4.88 g/cm3 à High detection efficiency

## – At 15 cm thick, nearly 100% efficient for

## gammas up to 10 MeV [2]

## Problem

11/17/20 Los Alamos National Laboratory

## • ~80% of the total light output consists of slower (600 ns decay constant)

emission peaked at 310 nm [2] – Low count rate à slow component for energy resolution, fast component for timing – High count rate à pile up

5

<!-- Page 8 -->


## Goal

11/17/20 Los Alamos National Laboratory

## • To develop a BaF2-based detector that leverages the fast emission

## component for optimal timing characteristics

– Rare earth doping (e.g., La, Ce, Y) suppresses the slow component – Bandpass filters can selectively transmit the fast component to a photodetector

## 5. PET-like source localization

11/17/20 Los Alamos National Laboratory

## • One BaF2 array on either side of a 22Na source

– Alternatively, one BaF2 array and the LYSO array • Can potentially build larger arrays with more PLANACONS

## • Goal: to measure the difference in times-of-arrival for coincident

annihilation photons – Entirely determined by geometry, i.e., distance from source to each detector – Source localization in 3D space
